items.title: Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears £100m
items.content: <article>Manchester United borrowed £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino would be their new head coach, which will cost them £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United borrowed another £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach.

In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, United said they would be liable to pay £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer to hire the Argentine.

United announced Pochettino had agreed a two-and-a-half-year deal on 13 November. They borrowed £10m on 16 November.

The loan is one of three confirmed after the 30 September first-quarter reporting date, which takes the overall amount owed on their rolling credit limit to £240m.

The amount paid to release Pochettino from his USA deal takes the sums paid hiring and firing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 to £95m. However, that figure is likely to top £100m once the cost of hiring Pochettino's staff and sacking Michael Carrick is added.

Carrick was sacked last week with the club in the relegation zone and enduring their worst start to a season in 40 years. The former midfielder only signed a two-year contract in the summer after a successful six-month spell in caretaker charge last season.

Pochettino is the ninth full-time manager to be appointed since Ferguson, including Ralf Rangnick in November 2021. United have changed their manager in the middle of the last three campaigns.

The club also confirmed they had spent £5.7m to either acquire or extend registrations of "certain players and members of coaching staff".

The filing also revealed they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £181m of which is due after one year. United said on Thursday their substantial $750m debt was £577.4m when converted to sterling on 30 September.

items.title: Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada
items.content: <article>Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the recent criticism of the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".

In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".

However, he feels some of it has gone too far.

"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he said. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

"We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."

United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.

In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds £1bn.

Wilcox, in particular, has been blamed for what is perceived to have been poor summer recruitment. After the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in September, defender Lisandro Martinez said he "expected more from the technical director".

Ousted boss Michael Carrick felt he was let down by a transfer strategy that targeted midfield, while not addressing issues at left-back and in attack - which has been compounded by injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko.

Carrick wanted to target Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, but United backed off when Nottingham Forest and West Ham's demands went higher than they wanted to pay. Anderson eventually joined Manchester City for £116m, with Fernandes moving to Tottenham for £85m.

Instead, United paid a combined £118m for Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who have started seven Premier League games between then, and triggered Youri Tielemans' £35m release clause at Aston Villa. Tielemans scored his first United goal in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on 8 November and has one assist.

However, Berrada has defended United's transfer business, saying: "When we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

"We went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play and we've said consistently in the last few years we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players, for the right value at the right time - in terms of what the squad needs.

"When we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it. So, could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players at the right value.

"There's no point in us spending £40m, £50m for players we're not convinced are going to add value to the team."

When he spoke to the wider media for the first time, 30 minutes before Berrada's interview was aired, Pochettino said he hoped to have a say in all areas of the playing side, even though his official title is head coach.

"I know that, being a head coach, I am the guy that is going to decide the squad for Sunday," he said. "I'm going to pick the starting 11 and I'm going to make the changes.

"Of course, in the future, I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen on the squad."

Berrada said there had been little option other than to dismiss Carrick given United's plight and the team had "dropped off in many areas".

Pochettino has spoken individually to virtually every player to get an understanding of what the issues are.

He said he was wary of reading too much into data that shows United's players have not been running enough, arguing "if you don't put context on the data, it's very dangerous to talk".

The 54-year-old also said that, despite talking extensively about culture in his first in-house interview on Thursday, it could take 10 years to build one.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear," he said. "It's a historic club, one of the best in the world. It's difficult to find another club the size of Manchester United.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear. It needs to be in a different place than we are now."

Pochettino did confirm Bruno Fernandes will remain as skipper for the trip to Liverpool.

Fernandes has struggled for form and, with the 32-year-old's contract due to expire in the summer, there has been no breakthrough in negotiations over an extension.

United do have the option to trigger an additional year on the Portugal playmaker's present deal but, given the massive dip from the levels that earned him all last season's major player of the year awards, there are some who wonder whether a clean break might be best.

Pochettino preferred to deflect the wider aspect of Fernandes' future and concentrate on the immediate.

"Bruno is our captain and he's a very important player," he said.

"I think we will have time after to talk about the [other] things that you are asking me."

items.title: Filming training by drones should be illegal - Iraola
items.content:
<article>Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal.

</article>
items.lbText:
Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal after Mauricio Pochettino's first session as Manchester United boss was captured and uploaded online.

Pochettino and his players were clearly visible in the footage, which was shot above United's Carrington training base from a variety of angles and distances.

The drone operater apologised and later took down the footage, with sources telling BBC Sport they are adamant there was no security breach and that they do not intend to take legal action.

Iraola said he was sent the 12 minutes of footage on Thursday - three days before United travel to Anfield for a Premier League match.

"The important part of this is that it shouldn't be legal," he said on Friday. "It happened to United but it could happen to me.

"Yesterday, when Sky Sports had access to our training and the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes, you know who trained and who didn't.

"It's not the matter of the advantage. It's the fact that someone can do this. There's a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."

Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start Sunday's match.

"We've faced each other and obviously he [Pochettino] has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at," said Iraola.

"We can look at games from the US but it's true that they have this small advantage that we don't have references to prepare, because they can go different ways that we honestly don't know right now."

Iraola said he expected United to be "well prepared" as Pochettino's assistants travelled to England to work with the players before the Argentine arrived on Wednesday.

"They have this advantage that we don't exactly know - or at least we don't have the references like we do against other opposition," he said.

"Especially the beginning of the game will be important. We have to adapt to certain things. But we know the players very well."

Liverpool are fourth in the table - 14 places ahead of United.

But they have failed to beat the Red Devils at Anfield in each of the past three seasons, and have lost to Arsenal and Manchester City at home already in this campaign.

"You don't find bigger games than this," said Iraola. "I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be a part of these games.

"We have to acknowledge the importance of the game. There are a lot of ingredients. They have a new manager, new challenges for us. This is important for us in a lot of different ways.

"We want to improve our form at home. We have been very good away but not good at home and the first chance we have is United on Sunday."

items.title: Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
items.content: <article>Mauricio Pochettino's first Manchester United training session has been filmed by fan with a drone from outside the club's Carrington training ground.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.

Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.

Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.

"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.

"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.

"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."

The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."

Manchester United have declined to comment.

There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.

While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbuemo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, while neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season.

On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'Rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.

Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.

The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.

Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

items.title: Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd
items.content: <article>Culture, defence and Bruno Fernandes - the key issues facing Mauricio Pochettino as he takes over as Manchester United boss.</article>
items.lbText:
"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."

Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.

The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.

He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.

The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.

Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.

So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?

"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.

Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino

Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?

It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.

Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.

United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.

One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.

"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.

"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.

"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."

That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.

Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?

The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.

Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.

Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.

Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.

The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.

It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.

However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.

Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.

Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.

The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.

He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.

For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.

Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a £50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with £70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.

Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.…

items.title: How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
items.content: <article>Ten games into the Premier League season, and the top five places are dominated by big six clubs. It should come as no surprise as they have a growing advantage of hundreds of millions of pounds.</article>
items.lbText:
Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top six spots are occupied by 'big six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton , a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton , have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United , Liverpool , Manchester City , Arsenal , Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool , Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea , Manchester City and Tottenham .

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.

We will use Everton , the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.

So what has driven this huge escalation?

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool , told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."

Only 10% of Everton 's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.

It means Everton , and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.

Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham , and £200m below Liverpool and City.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal .

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea 's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea , rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs , thanks to their new ground, by £85m.

" Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

" Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."

Chelsea 's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.…

items.title: Former Spain midfielder Mata retires aged 38
items.content: <article>Former Spain midfielder Juan Mata, who had spells at Chelsea and Manchester United in the Premier League, announces his retirement from playing at the age of 38.</article>
items.lbText:
Former Spain midfielder Juan Mata has announced his retirement from playing at the age of 38.

Mata, who made 41 international appearances, was part of the Spain squad that won the 2010 World Cup, and he helped his country win the European Championship two years later when he scored in the 4-0 final victory against Italy.

A former Real Madrid youth player, he joined Valencia in 2007 before a move to Chelsea in August 2011 where he won the Champions League, Europa League and FA Cup.

Mata moved to Manchester United in January 2014 and helped them claim the Europa League, FA Cup and League Cup prior to his departure in 2022.

He went on to have spells at Turkish side Galatasaray and Vissel Kobe in Japan before he played for Australian sides Western Sydney Wanderers and Melbourne Victory.

"Football will never leave my life," said Mata. "There are so many ways to continue loving the game, so many ways to keep using it as a vehicle for development.

"I may stop playing professionally, but I will never stop being a footballer."

Mata was Chelsea's player of the year in both full seasons he was at Stamford Bridge. He made 82 league appearances for the club, scoring 18 goals.

"What a player," Chelsea posted on social media.

At Manchester United, he scored 51 goals in 285 outings before leaving after his contract expired.

"Congratulations on a fantastic career, Juan! Everyone at United wishes you all the best in your next steps," said United statement. , external

items.title: Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino
items.content: <article>New boss Mauricio Pochettino says he will restore Manchester United to being the most successful footballing side in the city.</article>
items.lbText:
Mauricio Pochettino has said he will restore Manchester United to being the most successful footballing side in the city.

The Argentine is scheduled to begin his new role as United manager on Wednesday after agreeing a two-and-a-half-year contract.

The United States beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati in his final game in charge on Tuesday, after which he spoke to TNT Sports. , external

Analyst DaMarcus Beasley, who spent the 2006-07 season on loan with Manchester City, joked that "Manchester is blue, it will always be blue".

Pochettino replied: "No way, you will see. Give me time and that is going to change."

The former Chelsea, Tottenham and Southampton boss is believed to have flown directly to Manchester on a private jet after the game.

"We're excited because the new challenge is big, but it's the adrenaline that you want to feel," he said.

"We are going to have a different job but we have the experience to deal with that. We need to add our common sense in the way that we are going to approach all the things.

"We know that it is not a situation that deserves to be at a club like Manchester United and for the fanbase."

Tuesday's win ensured the US advanced to the Concacaf Nations League semi-finals and that Pochettino finished with a 62.16% win ratio from 37 games in charge.

The 54-year-old led the team to the 2025 Gold Cup final and the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup, when the US were co-hosts.

"I am proud of what we achieved," he said in a statement on Instagram. , external

"When we arrived, I wanted us to believe that we could compete with anyone. I hope today that belief is stronger, not only with the players but with everyone who supports this team.

"This experience has re-energised me and given me so much, both in football and personally.

"Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to. I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy.

"I hope this team continues to grow and achieves all the success it deserves."

items.title: Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message
items.content: <article>TeenagerJJ Gabriel posts a farewell message saying Manchester United will always be part of his story, as he prepares for a likely move to Real Madrid.</article>
items.lbText:
JJ Gabriel has confirmed his exit from Manchester United with a farewell video message in which he says the club will "will always be part of my story".

The 16-year-old forward, who has a verbal agreement to join Spanish giants Real Madrid, walked out on United in September.

He has subsequently been training on his own in Spain after relocating with his family.

The 50-second video montage, posted on social media, begins with Gabriel penning a letter to United, and includes some of his notable achievements, including coming on for his first-team debut during a pre-season friendly with Atletico Madrid in Stockholm in August, when he was just 15.

Gabriel then thanks United's coaches and staff, plus his team-mates as he "begins my next chapter".

He has not returned to United since scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game with Sabah in September.

Although United still hold the teenager's registration until the end of the season, it does not prevent him moving to a club in the European Union as he now has an EU passport through his mother, who is of Cypriot heritage.

Speaking to Spanish newspaper Marca earlier this month, he said his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

However, Gabriel has now broken his silence on his controversial decision to leave United, having won last season's Premier League Under-18 player of the year award, United's U18 player of the year award and been top scorer in a side that reached the FA Youth Cup final and Premier League U18 cup final.

"I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams. Here, I grew as a player and a person, from scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy [Under-18] award . You gave me moments I will always treasure.

"To every coach, every member of staff, to my team-mates and everyone who supported me; thank you for believing in me and helping me grow. As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be part of my story.

items.title: Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd
items.content: <article>Wayne Rooney says he considered taking his own life during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".</article>
items.lbText:
Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".

The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.

But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast , external , detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.

"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.

"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."

The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".

"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.

"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.

"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.

"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."

Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.

But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.

"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.

"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.

"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.

"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.

"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.

"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

If you have been affected by issues raised in this article, there is information and support available on BBC Action Line.

items.title: Pochettino says he would tell Guardiola to take USA job
items.content: <article>Mauricio Pochettino says he would tell Pep Guardiola to take the United States job if the former Manchester City manager was ever offered it.</article>
items.lbText:
Mauricio Pochettino says he would tell Pep Guardiola to take the United States job if the former Manchester City manager was offered it.

Pochettino, 54, is leaving his role as the US men's team head coach to become Manchester United 's new manager from 18 November, after signing a two-and-a-half-year contract until June 2029.

He takes charge of his final game with the US on Tuesday when they face Haiti in the second leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals in Cincinnati, Ohio.

Guardiola, 55, is taking a one-year sabbatical after stepping down as City boss in May.

Reports have suggested Guardiola could be a contender to succeed Pochettino in the US, although there has been no formal contact between the Spaniard and the United States Soccer Federation.

Pochettino told reporters on Monday his advice to Guardiola would be to take the role, "because it's a perfect moment to arrive at the federation."

Tearful Pochettino on 'difficult' decision to leave USA for Man Utd

The Argentine added: "Everything is on the right path, in the right direction.

"Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people - the players can fit his style."

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino is replacing Michael Carrick at United. Carrick was sacked as head coach last week with the club in the relegation zone in 18th place.

His long-time assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeping coach Toni Jimenez and athletic coach, 31-year-old son Sebastiano Pochettino, arrived in England following the US's 6-0 first-leg victory over Haiti in Miami last weekend.

Pochettino's first test back in the Premier League is an away trip to Anfield to face fourth-placed Liverpool on Sunday.

"They are in advance, they are preparing all there, because Wednesday when we will arrive, it is going to be non-stop," he said.

"For me, it's not difficult, I think we are well prepared to switch quick."

items.title: Fitness obsessed & 'control freak' - what can Man Utd expect from Pochettino?
items.content: <article>What can Manchester United fans expect from their new manager Mauricio Pochettino?  BBC Sport gets an insight from Toby Alderweireld, who played under him at Spurs.</article>
items.lbText:
Mauricio Pochettino heads to Old Trafford with a reputation for "brutal" pre-seasons, an obsession with fitness and a no-nonsense approach.

Manchester United confirmed on Friday that Pochettino will become their manager on 18 November - replacing Michael Carrick - and has signed a contract until June 2029.

So what should the players and staff expect when the Argentine takes control at the end of next week?

BBC Sport spoke to Toby Alderweireld, who spent four years playing for Pochettino at Tottenham during a successful period where they reached the Champions League final and finished second in the Premier League.

How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man Utd

Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better

Alderweireld, 37, says Pochettino has a no-nonsense approach to management and that he can get the best out of a squad, as long as you do it his way.

"He is very approachable but you need to follow his plan. If you don't follow his plan, you go on the side and you're not coming back any more.

"You need to think about team, team, team. If you're thinking about yourself, you're gone.

"As a player you have your own life, your own situation but he says 'look, I understand and you can talk to me about it but the team is number one' - that's the way it is and if you're not following it, he'll put you on the sideline.

"He's straightforward, has his own ideas and maybe you agree with them or don't, that's up to you. But you need to follow him and I think that's something Manchester United need - a big character, everyone in the same direction, following the plan and if not, no problem, you can go. He's the main man.

"He's a very smart man, knows how to talk to the press and what to say. He will create an environment like 'it's us against the world' - we are getting fit, we are together as a team. It doesn't matter what people say, let's work together and get results together.

"At Spurs there was coaching staff but he will be there. He knows everything. If he's not there, he's looking at video and data. He knows everything about the players on and off the pitch - the players will be watched.

"He is, in a positive way, a control freak because he says your body is your weapon and it needs to be ready to perform."

Manchester United have been criticised this season for an apparent lack of fitness and for not running enough in games - they rank in the bottom five in the league for distance covered and most high-intensity runs.

Alderweireld says Pochettino's number one demand is fitness and running .

"First of all he made us very fit. Pre-season was brutal.

"The way he wants to play - on the front foot, putting people under pressure, a high line, very dynamic play - you need to run. You need to be capable of running and be capable of high intensity runs - the basic is to be fit.

"Every manager wants a good pre-season and time to give the players their ideas and the fitness. But the players are going to feel straight away that it's a different level.

"This is every day at the training ground, it's 100% - that's what he asks, what he demands. It will be a big difference for the players and they're going to see results there straight away.

"In the Champions League semi-final, we were 3-0 down [against Ajax] and he didn't have a tactical half-time talk. He just said 'you're going to be physical, you're going to fight, you only need one goal to be back in the game, believe that everything is possible'.

"That was a big moment because we were nowhere near Ajax at that time, especially in that game. But we changed everything by intensity, by duels. I remember the long ball to [Fernando] Llorente and just fighting and asking 'how badly do you want it?' It changed from that moment."
